KEY MESSAGE 1...Warmest day of the week today, with dry weather 
persisting through Wednesday.

Heading into this afternoon, partly cloudy to mostly sunny skies are 
supporting temperatures to climb into the mid to upper 50s, whereas 
a blanket of cloud cover is passing south across the Watertown and 
Tug Hill region due to a passing shortwave and associated surface 
low across southern Quebec. Speaking of which, this low will 
continue to progress east reaching New England this evening, 
allowing for some synoptic scale forcing and lake induced 
instability across the North County and Saint Lawrence Valley this 
afternoon where a few embedded showers will be possible. 

Aside from the showers, it will continue to be breezy this 
afternoon with gusts of ranging from 25 to 35 mph due to a low-level 
jet of 30 to 40 knots across the eastern Great Lakes.

A weak ridge will slide east across the Mid-Atlantic tonight through 
Wednesday, supporting dry weather to persist through much of the day 
Wednesday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Unsettled and colder weather will return Wednesday 
night and last through the end of the week, where some minor wet 
snow will be possible mainly across higher terrain.

Upper level pattern will amplify Thursday through Friday as a strong 
ridge will build across the Rockies and a deep, broad trough digs 
south across much of the eastern CONUS. Meanwhile at the surface, an 
initial area of low pressure will pass across the Ohio Valley 
Wednesday night, before giving way to a secondary coastal low off the 
Mid-Atlantic coast by Thursday. Additionally to the north of the 
region, a stalled cold front will lie across southern Canada. The 
coastal low will then slide northeast Thursday night through 
Saturday off the shores of New England, reaching the Canadian 
Maritimes Saturday night.  

Large scale forcing will increase late Wednesday afternoon through 
Thursday as the closed low takes shape upstream, with significant 
height falls spreading east across the Great Lakes. This will 
combine with frontogenesis and deformation north of the initial low 
track supporting periods of light rain Wednesday night through 
Thursday across the region. Precipitation type will stay all rain 
through Thursday evening, with the possible exception of the highest 
terrain across the western Southern Tier and the North Country.

Thursday night through Saturday, cold air will deepen across the 
eastern Great Lakes as the surface low strengthens off the New 
England coast, and the mid level closed low matures overhead. The 
stronger synoptic scale forcing will focus along the New England 
coast and well east of our area, leaving a weakly forced moist 
northerly flow regime across the eastern Great Lakes. Abundant wrap 
around moisture will combine with lake induced instability and north 
to northeast flow to produce occasional showers through the period, 
with the best coverage across higher terrain from upslope 
enhancement.

The airmass will grow cold enough to allow the rain to mix with and 
change to wet snow across higher terrain Thursday night through 
Friday. The coldest air aloft will then arrive Friday night through 
Saturday, when lower elevations will have the best chance of a mix 
or change to wet snow. The lack of stronger synoptic scale forcing 
and short fetch northerly flow will likely keep precipitation rates 
light, and light wet snow falling on warm ground will struggle to 
accumulate. 

The latest probabilistic forecasts from the full ensemble suite of 
the NBM and LREF Grand Ensemble continue to suggest a high 
likelihood of very minor accumulations across higher terrain Friday 
through Saturday, but minimal chance of anything more than very 
minor impacts. Ensemble data suggests no accumulation for lower 
elevations including the main population centers of the region, 
however the these areas may see the first flakes of the winter 
season. 

This system will gradually pull away Sunday through Monday with a 
return to dry weather early next week. Cool temperatures will 
persist for a few days before a warming trend develops by the middle 
of next week.
